arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: General Wall argued the case should be dismissed. He stated the district court found an injury based on a chill in participation. He claimed that counting is now over. He asserted that any chill has fallen away. He argued there is no live or ripe case now. He suggested the Court should hold the case for a couple of weeks.

Ms. Underwood argued the Constitution requires apportioning House seats by the number of persons. She stated the President's policy refuses to count people in unlawful immigration status. She claimed this policy is flatly inconsistent with the constitutional command. She argued there is a substantial risk of injury.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The dispute centers on whether the President can exclude undocumented residents from the census. This exclusion affects how House seats are distributed among states.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The government wants the Court to dismiss the case as moot. It argues the census counting is already finished.
The states want the Court to block the exclusion policy. They argue it violates the constitutional requirement to count all persons.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government argues the case is over because the counting phase has ended. It claims any potential chill on participation no longer exists.
The states argue the policy violates the Constitution. They contend the law requires counting all persons regardless of immigration status.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Thomas asked if the issue is separate from the census itself.

Chief Justice Roberts asked if the December 31 deadline for transmitting census data is still operative. He asked if the Court needs to decide by that date. He also asked if the Court should assume the policy targets a specific subset of undocumented residents. He questioned whether the Court can intervene after the data is transmitted to the President.
